caption:
Etobicoke move-in. CO alarm law changed.

The Government of Ontario says Fire Code changes that took effect January 1, 2026 expand where carbon monoxide (CO) alarms must go in existing homes. 1) Homes with a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage need CO alarms on every storey, including storeys with no bedrooms. 2) Keep one adjacent to each sleeping area too, in the hallway outside the bedrooms. 3) In an owner-occupied home the homeowner is responsible for complying; in a rental, the landlord is. 4) Test CO alarms monthly and replace the batteries every year. Your local fire department can answer questions about your own home.
Source: Government of Ontario, "CO alarm requirements for existing homes" (Dec 2025) and "Carbon monoxide safety" (ontario.ca), checked Nov 23, 2026.

Milton seller. Multiple offers. Disclose?

The Real Estate Council of Ontario (RECO) explains the rules for competing offers. 1) The seller's Realtor® must tell every buyer who submitted a written offer how many competing offers there are. 2) Sharing the content of the offers is the seller's choice and only happens with the seller's written direction. 3) Personal or identifying information about the buyers cannot be shared. 4) A seller can change that direction at any time. Talk through your options with your Realtor® before offer night.
Source: RECO, "Dealing with competing offers" (seller page) and Bulletin 4.1 (reco.on.ca), checked Nov 23, 2026.

caption:
Caledon bidding war? Read this.

The Real Estate Council of Ontario (RECO) says the seller's Realtor® must tell every buyer with a written offer how many competing offers there are, and that the seller can choose whether the content of offers is shared. RECO also says a competing offer situation does not necessarily mean a home sells above asking, that an offer at or above asking will not guarantee acceptance, that pre-qualifying for a mortgage does not safely eliminate the need for a financing condition, and that skipping a home inspection condition is a significant risk. Talk through your limits with your Realtor® before offer night.
Source: RECO, "Competing offers" (buyer page, reco.on.ca), checked Nov 23, 2026.

$1.5M home. Down payment jumps.

New Reel on my page tonight: how much more cash the minimum down payment needs when a price crosses one line. Take a guess first.

Planning a move? Comment INFO to get full details, or call 905-452-4298.

Krishna Rander, Realtor® | PROPERTY.CA INC., Brokerage

#GTArealestate #downpayment #keyswithkrishna

$10K more price. $176K more down.

Example only, using the minimum down payment table from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada:
1) $1,490,000 home: 5% of the first $500,000 = $25,000.
2) 10% of the other $990,000 = $99,000, so $124,000 down in total.
3) $1,500,000 home: 20% down = $300,000.
That is $176,000 more cash down for $10,000 more on the price ($300,000 - $124,000). FCAC's table: 5% of the first $500,000, plus 10% of the portion from $500,000 to $1.5 million; 20% at $1.5 million or more. Closing costs and any mortgage insurance premium are extra, and your lender may ask for more, so confirm your numbers with your lender.

caption:
Older Mississauga home. Insurance denied?

The Electrical Safety Authority (ESA) says knob-and-tube wiring was used in homes in the early 1900s to the 1940s, and that many insurers will not provide or renew coverage on homes with this type of wiring; some may ask you to replace it first. 1) Know the era of the home. 2) Ask an insurer about the wiring before you finalize a purchase. 3) ESA recommends an assessment by a Licensed Electrical Contractor, which is different from a home inspection because it focuses only on the electrical. 4) Make sure anyone doing electrical work can legally do it in Ontario.
Source: Electrical Safety Authority, "Knob and Tube Wiring" (esasafe.com), checked Nov 23, 2026.

caption:
Pretty kitchen. Wrong street.

A tired kitchen can be updated; a location can't be moved. 1) The mistake: choosing a home because the kitchen looks great. 2) Paint, floors and kitchens can be updated over time. 3) You can't move the street, and the roof, wiring and foundation can be costly to fix. 4) Ask your home inspector about the big items before you fall for the finishes.

caption:
Georgetown basement unit. Registered?

The Town of Halton Hills says no one may operate or permit the occupancy of an additional residential unit (ARU) unless it is registered, and its guide lists fines of up to $50,000 for individuals. Registration involves inspections by Fire, Building and Municipal Law Enforcement. If a home you are buying has a basement apartment, ask to see the registration and any building permits, and check the details with the Town's Building Services. Rules vary by municipality.
Source: Town of Halton Hills, "Additional Residential Unit (ARU) Registration Guide" (haltonhills.ca, updated 2025), checked Nov 23, 2026.
